claims.evidence: GOSH page: used mainly for nausea/vomiting from chemotherapy or radiotherapy, and also after surgery.
StatPearls ondansetron entry: peripheral actions (vagal nerve terminal 5-HT3 receptors) thought to be the predominant antiemetic mechanism.
Ondansetron StatPearls entry (NBK499839): central effects via antagonism of 5-HT3 receptors in the area postrema. The draft attributed this to NBK513318 only; attribution corrected to NBK499839.
claims.newSentence: The ondansetron StatPearls entry describes an additional central action on 5-HT3 receptors in the area postrema, a region of the brain stem. (cite NBK499839, not NBK513318)

claims.evidence: StatPearls selective 5-HT3 antagonists entry: labelling warns of serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic drugs; evidence limited.
MedlinePlus lists headache; GOSH lists headache as commonly noted.
MedlinePlus lists constipation; GOSH notes constipation can occur.
MedlinePlus tablet page lists weakness, tiredness, drowsiness.
GOSH: sensations of warmth or flushing, particularly in the head or over the stomach.
Notts APC sheet: hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia should be corrected prior to ondansetron; also in UK SmPCs and MHRA.

Search could not confirm the full MedlinePlus ondansetron list (chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting); only blurred vision/vision loss and fast/slow/irregular heartbeat were confirmed on the tablet page as serious effects, plus general advice for immediate medical care. Full list came only from a non-MedlinePlus consent form.
claims.newSentence: MedlinePlus lists vision changes and a fast, slow or irregular heartbeat among serious effects needing urgent medical attention; in the UK, call 999 in an emergency, or contact NHS 111 or a GP for advice.

notes: Seven searches used. Wording across items stays free of doses and numeric cut-offs. cautions[4] relates to the IBS-D off-label sheet but the electrolyte point is also in UK SmPCs.
